summary:
Tomsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender transition is banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no discrimination protection is available to transgender people. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) applies this framework to Tomsk Oblast and records no facts specific to the oblast.

For a trans visitor, that note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, but that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It also identifies people in the North Caucasus in the same category. The practical consequence for a visitor is exposure to the extremist-designation regime and the propaganda statutes, which carry arrest, detention and deportation for foreigners.

Enforcement is documented and current. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols: 98 administrative and 3 criminal, with at least 20 people facing criminal charges since January 2024. Repeat display of the banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) recorded a further escalation in the severity of the charges: three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment. The same report shows the designation operating through both the administrative and criminal codes, so low-level encounters such as a stop or a search can convert into an extremism matter.

The UK Home Office note counts 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024, a figure covering the whole country rather than Tomsk Oblast. That count sits alongside the 101 convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch, and the two sources use different measurement bases, so they should not be read as a single tally.

The divergence between the two risk assessments matters for planning: general risk for LGB people is not established at the level of persecution, while the risk for trans people and public LGBT+ advocates is. A trans visitor therefore faces a higher assessed risk than the same visitor assessed as LGB alone.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tomsk Oblast have no legal means of changing the gender marker on official documents, since legal gender recognition was banned nationally in 2023, and no route to legal gender-affirming care, which has been effectively banned since the same year. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no statutory anti-discrimination protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation.

Residents also fall within the extremism regime described by Human Rights Watch: 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions had been issued by 30 June 2025 for participation in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or display of its symbols, with repeat display carrying up to four years in prison. The UK Home Office note counts 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

For residents, the Home Office note assesses trans people and public LGBT+ advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention. That standard governs UK asylum claims brought from Tomsk Oblast.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tomsk Oblast-specific facts appear in the source inventory. The note records none, and no oblast-level enforcement data, incident reports, detention figures or facility information for Tomsk is sourced here; every enforcement figure used is national.

The two source counts are not reconciled: the Home Office figure of 139 people impacted between 2022 and 2024 and the Human Rights Watch figure of 101 convictions by June 2025 measure different things over overlapping periods, and the sources do not state how they relate.

Whether any local authority in Tomsk Oblast has taken oblast-specific measures, whether any hospital continues to provide gender-affirming care despite the national ban, and how the extremism designation has been applied by courts in this oblast are unresolved and not sourced in this inventory.
